designs.name: L-4
designs.summary: A small, square, one-room cabin built to live and watch from at the same time, with windows wrapping all four walls so the lookout could see in every direction. It is the design most people picture when they think of a fire lookout; sources count well over a thousand built.

years_in_use.text: Roughly 1929 to 1953. Sources agree a prototype existed by 1929 and that the design was formally approved and refined between 1930 and 1936, then stayed in standard use until about 1953, when the flat-roofed R-6 design began to replace it.

designs.cab_size: 14 x 14 ft, about 6 ft 9 in to the eaves
designs.tower_heights: Could sit directly on the ground or on a wooden tower; Forest Service tower plans for use with the L-4 came in 10-ft increments from 10 ft up to about 120 ft, with a 3-ft-wide catwalk around the cab when raised on a tower.
designs.materials: Wood frame construction, drop or rustic siding on the lower third of the walls, cedar shingle or similar roofing, wood sash windows, and hinged exterior wood shutters.
makers: USDA Forest Service (standard agency design, not a commercial manufacturer)
designs.regions: Built nationwide but most numerous in USFS Region 1 (Montana/Idaho) and Region 6 (Washington/Oregon); well over a thousand were erected.
features: square one-room cabin, windows on all four walls
hip (pyramidal) roof on most surviving examples; earliest ones had a plain gable roof
wide hinged wooden shutters that fold down to cover the windows when the cabin is unmanned
often sits atop a wood tower with a narrow catwalk porch
sometimes called 'Aladdin' because pre-cut kits for Region 6 were fabricated at a mill in Vancouver, Washington
the plain gable-roofed earliest version is sometimes nicknamed a 'grange hall' style cab
designs.uncertain: Sources disagree about where the L-4 originated. A Montana/Idaho National Register form credits Clyde Fickes of Region 1 with the first 14x14 prototype around 1929-1930, approved in 1931, later copied and revised by Region 6 in 1936. A Washington State National Register form instead describes the plan as adopted by Region 6 in 1929-30 and evolving out of Region 6's own earlier lookout plans going back to about 1915, with Region 1 treated as an adopter rather than the inventor. A compiler citing veteran lookout historian Ray Kresek says both regions produced similar 1929 plans independently and it is hard to say who was first. The two main National Register sources also give slightly different years for the roof-shape change (1931 vs. 1932) and for the shutter-hardware change (1936 is consistent, but described slightly differently). Treat the exact priority and exact revision years as unsettled.

designs.name: L-5
designs.summary: A smaller relative of the L-4, used at lesser lookout points where a full-size cabin was not needed. The name was applied to more than one actual building, so what an 'L-5' looks like varies by forest.

years_in_use.text: Mainly built during the 1930s; sources do not give a clear end date.

designs.cab_size: Nationally described as 10 x 10 ft, a scaled-down L-4. In USFS Region 1 (Montana/Idaho), however, period Forest Service records instead describe 'L-5' as a 14 x 14 ft gable-roofed log cabin, not a 10x10 frame building.
designs.tower_heights: Normally built on the ground, as a low-priority secondary lookout point.
designs.materials: Wood frame construction for the 10x10 version; peeled-log construction with a gable roof for the Region 1 variant.
designs.regions: Used at secondary lookout points nationwide; the 14x14 log-cabin variant is specifically documented in Idaho and Montana.
features: small, plain, single-room cabin
gable roof (both the 10x10 frame version and the Region 1 log version)
noticeably smaller than an L-4 if it is the 10x10 version
designs.uncertain: There is a real contradiction in the sources about size: most general design-type pages describe the L-5 as a 10x10 ft frame cabin, but a 1938 Forest Service inventory reproduced in the Montana/Idaho National Register form lists 'L-5' as a 14x14 ft gable-roofed log cabin built in 1930, which is the same footprint as an L-4 but in log rather than frame construction and with a gable instead of hip roof. A National Historic Lookout Register glossary entry gives only '10-by-10 cab' with no further detail. It is possible the name was reused for two different local building types; this page cannot resolve which is 'the' L-5.

designs.name: L-6
designs.summary: The smallest of the standard Forest Service cabins, built for a single observer to stand watch in rather than to live in day-to-day. It was usually perched high on a wooden tower, with the lookout's actual living quarters in a separate building on the ground below.

years_in_use.text: Documented as built from the early 1930s onward (a 1938 inventory lists examples dated 1932); sources do not give a clear end date.

designs.cab_size: 8 x 8 ft (one glossary source gives 8 ft 9 in square for an earlier, similarly named patrol shelter)
designs.tower_heights: Built on tall wooden towers, with the observer's separate living cabin at ground level; one documented example stood on a 50-ft pole tower.
designs.materials: Wood frame construction, hip roof on the standard version.
designs.regions: Documented in USFS Region 1 (Idaho/Montana); likely used more broadly as part of the same family of standard plans as the L-4 and L-5.
features: very small single-room cab, built for watching rather than living
hip roof
sits high on a tall wood tower, separate from the lookout's living quarters on the ground
designs.uncertain: One source describes the original 1935 handbook version as an '8 3/4 ft-square' shelter also called a 'Patrol Shelter or Tower Cupola,' while design-type summaries give a plain 8x8 ft figure; these may be the same building rounded differently, or an early vs. later version, but the sources do not say which.

designs.name: R-6
designs.summary: The design that replaced the L-4 from the 1950s onward. Instead of a peaked roof, it has a flat roof that overhangs the walls on all sides to shade the windows, giving lookouts of this type their distinctive squared-off silhouette.

years_in_use.text: Became the standard replacement design starting in 1953; individual examples were still being built into the 1970s.

designs.cab_size: Most general sources give 15 x 15 ft as the standard size, but numerous individually documented R-6 cabs are 14 x 14 ft instead.
designs.tower_heights: Often built on a base of concrete block, or on a concrete-pad foundation, rather than on a wood tower; at least one documented example sits on a 41-ft wood tower.
designs.materials: Plywood construction with a tar-paper roof covering in at least one description; later examples used concrete block for the base or tower as heavier materials became easier to transport.
makers: USDA Forest Service (standard agency design, Region 6)
models: Plan B-4300 / R-6 Flat (1959, 1964 and 1971 drawing revisions are documented)
designs.regions: Originated in and named for USFS Region 6 (Washington and Oregon); used there and adopted elsewhere as the L-4 was phased out, including Region 1 (Montana/Idaho).
features: flat roof that overhangs the cab walls by a few feet on all sides
square floor plan, usually 14x14 or 15x15 ft
often sits on a concrete-block base rather than a wood tower
designs.uncertain: Sources disagree on the standard cab size: general reference pages say 15x15 ft, but several individually documented R-6-style lookouts (for example on the Mt. Hood National Forest) are 14x14 ft, and one source describes a 12x12 ft cab being replaced in 1981 by a 14x14 ft 'R-6 wood flat top' cab. It is unclear whether 14x14 and 15x15 were both official variants, whether the standard changed over time, or whether 'R-6 style' was applied loosely to any flat-roofed replacement cab regardless of exact size.

designs.name: D-6
designs.summary: An early standard design that looks like a small two-story house: a plain lower story topped by a smaller, mostly-glassed second story the observer stood in. It predates the L-4 and is one of the oldest standardized Forest Service lookout shapes.

years_in_use.text: The prototype was built in 1915; most construction described in sources happened during the 1920s, with at least one individually dated example from 1917 and another from 1919. Sources do not give a clear end date for new construction, though the design was being phased out and replaced by the L-4 by the 1930s-1950s.

designs.cab_size: Main floor about 12 x 12 ft, with a second-floor observatory roughly a quarter the size of the main floor.
designs.tower_heights: Normally built directly on the ground or on a low base, as a two-story building rather than on a separate tower.
designs.materials: Wood frame construction, windows around the upper portion of the structure, hipped roof, glassed-in second story.
makers: USDA Forest Service (standard agency design, District/Region 6)
designs.regions: Originated in and named for District 6 (Pacific Northwest), later Region 6 (Washington and Oregon); also recorded as used in Idaho and Montana (Region 1). Very few examples remain standing today.
features: looks like a small two-story building rather than a single-room cab
glassed-in upper story (the 'cupola') sits on top of a larger plain lower story
hipped roof
usually built on the ground, not raised on a wood tower
designs.uncertain: The exact end date of D-6 construction is not clearly stated anywhere in the sources reviewed; it appears to have continued in occasional use into the 1920s even after the L-4 was introduced around 1929-1930, since Forest Service staff are recorded replacing D-6 cabins with newer L-4s only gradually, forest by forest.

designs.name: D-1
designs.summary: A log-built cousin of the D-6 cupola house, built of logs instead of milled frame construction but following the same two-story idea of plain quarters below and a glassed observation room above.

years_in_use.text: First built in 1922, per a glossary source; sources do not say how long the design stayed in use.

designs.cab_size: 14 x 14 ft log cabin with a framed glass cupola on top.
designs.tower_heights: Built on the ground, as a self-contained two-part log building rather than on a separate tower.
designs.materials: Peeled-log walls, with a framed, glassed cupola structure on top.
designs.regions: Documented in USFS Region 1 (an example is recorded under construction in Idaho's Powell Ranger District in 1922).
features: log cabin walls, not milled frame siding
glassed observation cupola on top of the main log structure
built on the ground
designs.uncertain: Only a single short glossary definition and one brief 1922 construction record were found for D-1; its relationship to D-6 (whether D-1 is simply a log version of the same basic D-6 idea, or a separately numbered plan from a different district) is not explained in the sources reviewed.

designs.name: Cupola houses (early regional plans)
aka: Old R-6 (pre-1930s, unrelated to the later flat-top R-6)
designs.summary: Before the L-4 became the nationwide standard around 1930, individual forests and regions built their own small two-part lookout houses: a plain room below and a glassed-in observation room or small tower above it, often called a cupola. These were usually log or frame cabins and varied a good deal from forest to forest.

years_in_use.text: Cupola-style lookouts were being built on some forests by around 1911; construction mostly tapered off through the 1930s as the L-4 and similar single-story plans became standard, though a few cupola cabins stayed in service for decades afterward.

designs.cab_size: Varied by forest and plan; documented examples include 12x12, 12x14, 14x14 and 15x15 ft.
designs.tower_heights: Built on the ground as self-contained two-part buildings, rather than on raised towers.
designs.materials: Both peeled-log and milled-frame construction are documented; roofs were typically hipped or gabled, with glazed sides on the upper cupola section.
makers: USDA Forest Service (various regional and district designs, not standardized nationally)
models: Old R-6 (12x12 frame with cupola, pre-dates the later flat-top R-6 of the same name)
R-3 log cabin with cupola (Flathead National Forest)
designs.regions: Documented mainly in USFS Region 1 (Idaho and Montana forests, including the Nez Perce, Flathead, Lolo and Bitterroot National Forests).
features: two-part building: a plain lower room with a smaller glassed cupola or crow's-nest room above
log or frame construction, often locally built rather than from a national kit
predates the single-story L-4-style cab
designs.uncertain: This entry groups together several different named plans (Old L-1, Old L-2, L-3, an early 'Old R-6,' the 'Nez Perce Model,' and an 'R-3' log cabin from the Flathead National Forest) that sources describe as closely related cupola-style buildings rather than as one single standardized plan. The exact differences between them, and the full nationwide extent of the cupola style outside Region 1, are not covered in the sources reviewed. Note that the 1920s-era 'Old R-6' cupola cabin is unrelated to the later (1953 onward) flat-roofed R-6 design, despite sharing a name.

designs.name: California (Region 5) plans
designs.summary: California's own Forest Service region developed its lookout standards somewhat independently of the Region 1/Region 6 L-4 story. It settled on its own 14x14 ft live-in cab in 1917, well before the L-4 existed, and later developed its own small all-steel cab for use on steel towers. The two families, wood cab and steel cab, were used side by side on different towers around the state.

years_in_use.text: The first standardized live-in cab (12x12 ft) was designed for Region 5 in 1914 and enlarged to 14x14 ft in 1917; that basic wood-cab lineage, and a later small steel-cab design adopted in 1951, both remained part of the region's standard plans for decades afterward.

designs.cab_size: 14 x 14 ft for the standard wood live-in cab (Plan 4-A, later revised as BC-301); 13 x 13 ft for the later all-steel live-in cab used on steel K-brace towers.
designs.tower_heights: Steel K-brace towers of this family were built up to about 120 ft; an individually documented example (North Mountain Lookout) used a 54-ft steel K-brace tower.
designs.materials: Early cabs were wood frame, pre-cut to standard dimensions ('ready-cut'); the later steel cab was built of ferrous sheet metal with a flat roof.
makers: USDA Forest Service Region 5 (standard agency design); Coert DuBois is credited as the original designer of the 1914/1917 cab
models: BC-1001 (1944-45 steel-frame cab with airport-control-tower-style sloped windows)
CL-30 / CL-104 (1951 all-steel 13x13 ft flat-roof cab)
Plan 809R (1947 California Department of Forestry octagonal cab)
features: 14x14 ft wood live-in cab on early examples, similar in size to an L-4 but independently developed
later steel K-brace towers topped with a small (13x13 ft) all-metal flat-roofed cab
some later examples (1944-45 'BC-1001' style) have outward-sloping windows reminiscent of an airport control tower
designs.uncertain: The scanned federal document this entry relies on has some OCR-garbled plan numbers for the region's steel-tower series (rendered inconsistently as, for example, 'L-20,' 'L-40' and 'L-80' in different passages), so exact plan numbers for the steel-tower-only (non-cab) designs are not given with full confidence here. It is also not fully clear from the sources how the 'CL-30' and 'CL-104' cab labels relate to each other -- they may be the same 13x13 ft steel cab design referred to by two different numbering systems, since both are described identically (13x13 ft, all-steel, flat roof) in the same source.

designs.name: Aermotor steel tower
designs.summary: A tall, open steel lattice tower topped by a small steel cab, built by a Chicago windmill maker that became the leading supplier of steel lookout towers before the Second World War. Other makers built towers to very similar specifications, so a maker's plate or local records are the surest way to tell an Aermotor from its look-alikes.

years_in_use.text: The Forest Service began buying Aermotor towers in 1912 (one source says the earliest sales were 1914); Aermotor was the leading maker of steel lookout towers through the 1920s and continued producing named models (such as the MC-39) at least into the mid-1930s. Sources do not state when Aermotor stopped building fire lookout towers specifically.

designs.cab_size: 7 x 7 ft steel cab, about 6 ft 9 in tall to the eaves.
designs.tower_heights: 1920s-era models ranged from about 21 to 102 ft (measured to the cab floor); a later design summary gives an overall range of 34 to 175 ft across all Aermotor tower models and heights.
designs.materials: Hot-dip galvanized steel throughout (coated after fabrication to resist rust), with a four-piece galvanized steel roof assembled from inside the cab and galvanized steel wall sheets on the lower part of the cab; window glass was not supplied by Aermotor and had to be sourced separately.
makers: Aermotor Company, Chicago, Illinois (a windmill and steel-tower maker founded in 1888)
designs.regions: Used nationwide; sources describe it as especially common in the southeastern, midwestern and eastern United States, and comparatively rare in the Pacific Northwest. Also documented on National Forests in Arizona and New Mexico.
features: open steel lattice tower with diagonal cross-bracing
small square steel cab (about 7x7 ft) at the top, enclosed with flat galvanized sheet panels below the window band
stairway or ladder running up the inside or outside of the tower, depending on model
frequent landing platforms with guardrails on the taller (LS-40) models
anchored to rock or concrete piers at the base with long galvanized anchor rods
designs.uncertain: Exact height ranges differ between sources (21-102 ft for 1920s models specifically, versus 34-175 ft given as an overall figure covering all eras/models), most likely because they are describing different time periods and model ranges rather than genuinely disagreeing. The precise meaning of Aermotor's model-letter codes (what 'L,' 'S,' 'X,' 'M,' 'C' stand for) is not explained in any source reviewed, so it is given here only as documented model names, not decoded abbreviations. A New York State National Register nomination states the Aermotor MC-39 model is 'essentially identical' to a 1933 International Derrick Company tower design, implying the two companies built to a shared or closely coordinated Forest Service specification rather than fully independent designs; this page treats Aermotor and IDECO as separate manufacturer entries because that is how the sources name them, while noting the overlap. One 2012 National Register form calls the 1930s maker 'the Aermotor Company of Texas'; company histories place Aermotor in Chicago in that era and its move to Texas decades later, so that wording looks like an anachronism.

designs.name: IDECO (International Derrick & Equipment Co.)
designs.summary: A steel lattice tower built by an Ohio company that normally made oil-well derricks and diversified into fire lookout towers. IDECO towers look very similar to Aermotor's, since both were built to closely related Forest Service specifications, but IDECO was a separate company based in Columbus, Ohio.

years_in_use.text: The company was founded in 1920; dated fire-tower plans from 1933 and 1937 were found, and the company was acquired by Dresser Industries in 1944, after which its further involvement in fire-tower production is not covered by the sources reviewed.

designs.tower_heights: A documented batch of five New York towers built in 1934 ranged from 59 to 79 ft; other sources describe individual IDECO towers at 80 and 100 ft.
designs.materials: Galvanized steel lattice tower and cab; one documented tower used structural steel produced by the Carnegie Steel Division of U.S. Steel.
makers: International Derrick & Equipment Company (IDECO), Columbus, Ohio, founded 1920; primarily a steel oil-well-derrick manufacturer; acquired by Dresser Industries in 1944
models: L-1401 (1937 design, associated with an Aermotor MC-99 tower in Forest Service records)
designs.regions: Documented in New Jersey, New York (Catskill and Adirondack regions) and Pennsylvania. Of nineteen IDECO towers recorded as erected in New York State, only eight remain on their original sites.
features: steel lattice tower, visually very close to an Aermotor tower
7x7 ft steel cab with eight windows, each with a nine-light steel sash
one pane on each face pivots open along a horizontal midline and is held by a notched steel catch bar
stairway typically zig-zags corner to corner up the tower
designs.uncertain: A New York National Register nomination states that Forest Service specifications for these towers were developed in coordination with 'the Aermotor Company of Texas,' and that the Aermotor MC-39 model is essentially identical to the 1933 IDECO model. As noted under the Aermotor entry, Aermotor did not relocate to Texas until decades after the 1930s, so that particular phrase in the source may be describing the company by its present-day location rather than its 1930s one. The same source also names two further companies -- Pacific Coast Steel and the Baker Manufacturing Company -- as having built towers to the same specifications, but gives no further detail on them.

designs.name: Other steel tower makers
designs.summary: Several other steel companies besides Aermotor and IDECO also supplied Forest Service lookout towers, mostly in the 1930s. They built to broadly similar specifications -- an open steel lattice tower topped by a small square steel cab -- so individual towers from these makers are hard to tell apart from Aermotor or IDECO towers without a manufacturer's plate or local records.

years_in_use.text: Documented examples date from the early-to-mid 1930s; the full date range each company was active in lookout-tower construction is not established by the sources reviewed.

designs.cab_size: 7 x 7 ft steel cab in all documented examples.
designs.tower_heights: Documented individual towers range from about 45 to 86 ft.
designs.materials: Galvanized or painted structural steel lattice construction, matching the general Aermotor/IDECO pattern.
makers: Blaw-Knox (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania steel-structures and construction-equipment manufacturer)
McClintic-Marshall (structural steel company; some sources instead spell the name 'McClintock-Marshall')
Pacific Coast Steel Company (named only in passing as a builder to Forest Service tower specifications)
Baker Manufacturing Company (named only in passing as a builder to Forest Service tower specifications)
designs.regions: Documented examples of Blaw-Knox towers are in Pennsylvania and West Virginia; documented examples of McClintic-Marshall towers are in Pennsylvania and New Jersey.
features: steel lattice tower with a small square steel cab, visually similar to Aermotor and IDECO towers
often erected by Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) crews in the 1930s
designs.uncertain: Sources spell the second company's name two different ways -- 'McClintic-Marshall' and 'McClintock-Marshall' -- without explaining which is correct; this looks like an orthographic error somewhere in the record rather than two different companies, but it could not be resolved from the sources reviewed. Depth of sourcing for these companies is much thinner than for Aermotor or IDECO: facts here come mainly from individual lookout-tower description pages rather than a company history, so company founding dates, headquarters details beyond the city, and total production are not available.
